body.body:
Fixes #670

## What happens

The progress bar shows `{eta_precise}` from indicatif, which estimates the remaining time as seconds per step multiplied by the steps that are left. A step of a hyperfine bar is a whole benchmark run, so that number only moves when a run starts or ends.

`hyperfine --runs 3 'sleep 5'` shows it:

- the initial run shows `ETA 00:00:00` for the whole five seconds
- when the next run starts, the ETA is 10 seconds instead of 5, because the run that took 5 seconds counts towards the average
- with a two hour run, the ETA stays at two hours until the run ends, and then it jumps up as the run that took hours counts towards the average

That is the increasing ETA and the "only shows a new ETA after a run is complete" from the report.

## What the change does

The bar now has its own `{remaining}` estimate:

- it predicts the remaining runs from the runs that finished, as the time each run took since the run before it finished
- it takes off the time that the line in progress has already taken
- while no run has finished yet, the ETA is the time of the current line, so the countdown starts at zero and goes up

The initial run is the first of those runs, because indicatif counts it as a step: the bar starts before it.

To know how long the running line has taken, the executors mark the start and the end of a line in a counter, and a timer in `Benchmark::run` turns that into the time of the line in progress. The marks are trait methods with default empty bodies, so an executor does not have to implement them.

The ETA is also capped at about 5 million years, past what a frame of the bar can show.

## How I checked it

`cargo test` passes (56 + 18 + 58 tests), and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.

The bar is drawn on a terminal only, so I ran it under a pty with `hyperfine --runs 3 --warmup 0 --shell=none 'sleep 3'` and read the redrawn lines:

| case | initial run | first line | second line |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| no hook | ETA 0, 1, 2, 3 | ETA 6 | ETA 3 |
| `--prepare 'sleep 2'` | ETA 0, 1, 2 | ETA 10 | ETA 5 |
| `--warmup 1` | ETA 0, 1, 2 | `Current estimate` and ETA 3 until the line ends | |

There is no integration test for this. `--style=basic` and `--style=none` replace the bar with a hidden one, so the tests cannot see its lines. The estimate itself, `format_remaining` and `Runs` in `src/output/progress_bar.rs`, is private and takes indicatif state that the tests cannot build. I can add a test for it if you want one: it needs a small split between the countdown and the estimate in this PR or a follow-up.

## Notes

The commits are separate on purpose:

1. The exit status check moves out of `run_command_and_measure_common`, so that the function does not grow an eighth argument (clippy has a limit of seven).
2. The executors count the lines they run, with the empty default methods on the trait.
3. The ETA and the timer use those counts.

`hyperfine --runs 1` has one run, so its countdown starts with that run.

body.title: Fix Org-mode export for commands with pipes

body.body:
In `src/export/markup.rs`, `MarkupExporter::table_results` escapes pipes with `\|` for every markup exporter:

```rust
let command = result.display_name.replace('|', \\|);
```

That works for Markdown and AsciiDoc, but Org-mode tables don't support backslash-escaping `|`. Any `|` inside a row splits the table cell, even after `\` or inside `=...=`.

For example, benchmarking a pipeline like `echo foo | wc -c` with `--export-orgmode` produces:

```org
| Command  |  Mean [ms] |  Change |  Factor |
|--+--+--+--|
| =echo foo \| wc -c=  |  ... |   |  |
```

Org-mode parses that data row as 5 columns (`=echo foo \`, `wc -c=`, ...) instead of 4, breaking the table layout and leaving unclosed `=` delimiters.

Pipe escaping probably belongs on each `MarkupExporter` implementation (defaulting to `\|` for Markdown/AsciiDoc, and handling Org-mode separately, e.g. `\vert{}`).

Observed on `master` (`c516152`).
body.title: --export-orgmode breaks table columns when a command contains |

body.body:
`--export-markdown`, `--export-asciidoc` and `--export-orgmode` interpolate `BenchmarkResult::display_name` into a table cell after escaping `|` only. A multi-line benchmark command, a `--command-name` containing CR/LF, or an unused parameter value with a line break therefore splits the row: the timing cells become a separate table row and the report is malformed, with no error.

This normalizes CRLF/CR/LF to spaces in the shared `table_results()` before the pipe escaping, so all three exporters stay intact. This only normalizes the export path; the terminal report is unchanged. A unit test feeds `first\r\nsecond\rthird\nfourth` through Markdown, AsciiDoc and org-mode and asserts there is no CR and the row stays whole; the CLI check for a real multi-line command produces one intact row in all three formats.

`cargo test --offline` (57 unit + 18 execution-order + 58 integration), `cargo fmt -- --check` and `cargo clippy --offline --locked --all-targets` pass. Baseline: the new test panics on raw CR/LF with the fix reverted.

AI assistance: prepared and tested with Claude Code.




CI note: the cross-target packaging jobs fail at the autocomplete copy step on this PR and on other PRs such as #1035; #1036 fixes that workflow. The code, tests and clippy jobs pass.

Commands currently finish all their measurements before the next command starts, so sustained load changes or thermal throttling can bias comparisons. Add `--interleave` to measure commands in round-robin order, while preserving each command's independent adaptive run count.

Closes #21.

- Extract resumable per-command benchmark state so the sequential and interleaved schedulers share measurement validation, hook execution, run-count estimation, reporting and result construction. Sequential execution remains the default.
- Alternate measured runs, remove completed commands from the rotation, keep per-command iteration numbers and show aggregate progress. Reports, comparisons and exports retain command order with the first command as reference.
- Run setup and warmups before each command's first measurement, prepare/conclude around every run, and cleanup immediately after its last measurement. Document that setup resources coexist and state changes needed on every switch belong in `--prepare`.
- Checkpoint file exports when a command completes and retain successful partial measurements when a later command or hook fails, including failures before any benchmark has finished.
- Document the option in the README, man page and changelog. Shell completions are generated from the updated CLI definition. No dependency changes.
- Fix the CI packaging lookup for both nested and legacy Cargo build-script output directories. The first upstream run compiled and passed its musl tests, then failed copying completions from the old layout. The updated Bash packaging block was checked against both layouts and rejects missing completion files even with stale staging contents. Debian packages reuse the staged completion files instead of assuming a Cargo output layout.

Validation on macOS arm64:

- Untouched-base `cargo +stable test --locked`: 132 tests passed.
- Three new execution-order tests initially failed because `--interleave` was unknown.
- Final `cargo +stable test --locked` (Rust 1.100) and `cargo +1.97.0 test --locked` (MSRV): all 140 tests passed on each toolchain.
- `cargo +1.97.0 clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo +1.97.0 fmt -- --check`: passed.
- New coverage includes three-command rotation, parameterized lifecycle hooks and warmups, single-run cleanup, independent adaptive counts (10 vs 4), exact equality of sequential/interleaved JSON measurements and statistics, initial/later failure exports, ignored failure exit codes, and checkpoint visibility to a subsequent command.
- Built-CLI demo with real Python subprocesses recorded `A:0 B:0 C:0 A:1 B:1 C:1 A:2 B:2 C:2`, with three successful JSON measurements per command.

Interleaving changes cache interactions, as documented. Windows/Linux execution will rely on upstream CI; the cross-platform tests include platform-specific shell commands.

For the Hyperfine 2.1 milestone.

Large parameter sweeps with file-based JSON export serialize all completed benchmarks again after each command. A 512-command sweep therefore serializes 131,328 result entries. This adds an opt-in `--export-json-lines FILE` that writes 512 entries for the same sweep. Consumers can read each completed benchmark while the next one is running.

Each line is a compact schema-v2 JSON document with a single result, with the same fields as the snapshot export. The writer flushes after each line. The existing snapshot exporter keeps its current behavior. Both formats can be requested together using separate paths.

### Measurements

End-to-end release builds on Apple Silicon, compared with master at c516152. Six paired trials per sweep size, alternating which binary ran first. Each variant spawned a real process twice. Timings below cover the entire invocation through the final write to a regular file.

| Variants | Snapshot JSON, median | JSON Lines, median | Median paired speedup |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8 | 17.0 ms | 16.3 ms | 1.04× |
| 512 | 1.799 s | 0.893 s | 2.03× |

Reproduce the larger workload with the baseline binary using the first command and the proposed binary using the second.

```sh
hyperfine --style=none -r 2 -P i 1 512 --export-json snapshot.json '/usr/bin/true {i}'
hyperfine --style=none -r 2 -P i 1 512 --export-json-lines records.jsonl '/usr/bin/true {i}'
```

This measures exporter overhead on short commands. In a four-variant Python top-k retrieval sweep (two runs per variant), both formats took about 0.46 s. With JSON Lines as the only exporter, the scheduler retains the first benchmark for comparisons and releases later measurements after flushing. In a real sweep of 128 commands with 64 process launches each, median peak RSS across three executions dropped from 8.00 to 6.86 MiB compared with the first JSON Lines commit. An isolated deterministic executor sweep (512 variants, 128 samples each) went from 11.47 to 2.72 MiB. Parameter expansion still allocates the command list up front.

### Verification

133 tests passed locally, including a regression test comparing both exports from the same run after a later command fails. The test checks that old contents are truncated and that completed records retain their order, measurements and statistical summaries. Release build, rustfmt and clippy also passed.

Parameter scans currently estimate their size as `(end - start + 1) / step`. This rejects `-P x 0 0 -D 0.000001` as too large even though it has one value, and accepts `-P x 0 300000 -D 3` despite its 100,001 values exceeding the 100,000-value limit.

Count the starting value after calculating the whole steps. Remove the remainder before dividing so Decimal rounding cannot add a nonexistent step, return zero for exhausted ranges, and check the final `usize` addition.

Validation: eight regression/control tests cover integer and decimal counts, exhausted iterators, both sides of the parameter limit, and large Decimal rounding. The original calculation failed six regression checks. `cargo test --locked` passes all 140 tests; `cargo fmt -- --check` and `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass on Rust 1.97.0. With posix_spawn, the child shares hyperfine's address space until exec, and the kernel carries hyperfine's peak RSS over into the child's ru_maxrss. Commands using less memory than hyperfine itself were reported with hyperfine's value (~3.2 MiB).

Use fork+exec instead (via a no-op pre_exec hook) when peak RSS is measured. A forked child only starts out with hyperfine's current anonymous memory (~1 MiB). Fork is slower to spawn, so time-only metric selections keep using posix_spawn.

Refs #988

With `--shell=none` the command line was split with POSIX rules, so on Windows a command like `C:\Windows\System32\where.exe /R C:\Windows\System32 notepad.exe` turned into `C:WindowsSystem32where.exe` and failed.

## Problem

`-n`/`--command-name` rejects a name that starts with a dash when the value is passed as a separate argument, for example `hyperfine -n "--shared-blocks" "ls"`. The `--command-name=--shared-blocks` form works, but the separate form is more natural and is how the equivalent `--parameter-scan` and `--parameter-list` options already behave.

## Change

Set `allow_hyphen_values(true)` on the `command-name` argument, matching the existing behaviour of `--parameter-scan` and `--parameter-list`.

## Testing

Added a unit test covering `-n --shared-blocks`. `cargo test` passes (58 integration tests and the full unit suite).

Closes #1017

body.title: Accept a --command-name value that starts with a dash

body.body:
`-n`/`--command-name` does not accept a value that starts with a dash when the value is passed as a separate argument:

```
$ hyperfine -N -r 2 -n "--shared-blocks" "ls"
error: unexpected argument '--shared-blocks' found

  tip: a similar argument exists: '--shell'

Usage: hyperfine -N --runs <NUM> --shell <SHELL> <command>...

For more information, try '--help'.
```

The `=` form works:

```
$ hyperfine -N -r 2 --command-name=--shared-blocks "ls"
Benchmark 1: --shared-blocks (2 runs)
```

A name without the similar-argument match gets a tip that does not apply here, since `-- --foo` would turn the name into a command:

```
$ hyperfine -N -r 2 -n "--foo" "ls"
error: unexpected argument '--foo' found
```

`--min-benchmarking-time` was parsed as an `f64` and used without any bound. The
run count is derived from it in `Benchmark::run`:

```rust
let runs_in_min_time = (self.options.min_benchmarking_time
    / (measurement.time_wall_clock + ...)).get::<ratio>() as u64;
```

`inf` is a valid `f64` literal, and casting an infinite float to `u64`
saturates, so the benchmark is asked for `u64::MAX` runs and never finishes.
Without an explicit `--max-runs` it has to be killed:

```
$ hyperfine --min-benchmarking-time=inf 'true'     # hangs
```

A non-positive value is meaningless rather than harmful. It collapses the
derived count to zero, which the run-bounds minimum then replaces, so it is
rejected in the same place.

hyperfine already refuses numeric arguments that cannot describe a benchmark
(an empty runs range; a zero or negative parameter-scan step), so this follows
what the other options do rather than introducing a new kind of check.

Added a unit test next to the existing options tests covering `inf`,
`infinity`, `nan`, `0` and `-1`, plus a positive value that still parses
through unchanged. It fails without the guard (I checked by removing the guard
and keeping the test).

One detail worth mentioning: a negative value can only be supplied as
`--min-benchmarking-time=-1`, because clap reads a bare `-1` as a flag. The
test uses that form.

`cargo test` (57 + 18 + 58) and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` are
clean; `cargo fmt --all --check` passes. No changelog entry, since CHANGELOG.md
has no unreleased section.

The README introduces decimal parameter scans as if `-D` were optional:

> This also works with decimal numbers. The `-D`/`--parameter-step-size` option can be used
> to control the step size

In the code, `-D` only has a fallback on the integer path. `get_parameter_scan_commands`
first tries to parse both bounds as `i32` and uses `step.unwrap_or("1")` (`src/command.rs:417-421`),
so an omitted step is fine for integer ranges. If either bound is not an integer it falls
through to the decimal branch, and there a missing step is a hard error:

```rust
if step.is_none() {
    return Err(ParameterScanError::StepRequired);
}
```

(`src/command.rs:436-438`), with the message "A step size is required when the range bounds
are floating point numbers. The step size can be specified with the
'-D/--parameter-step-size <DELTA>' parameter" (`src/error.rs:24`).

So `hyperfine -P delay 0.3 0.7 'sleep {delay}'` fails rather than picking a step, and the
`--help` text already models the required form (`src/cli.rs:246`,
`hyperfine -P delay 0.3 0.7 -D 0.2 'sleep {delay}'`). The wording now says the step size is
required for decimal ranges and mentions the integer default, keeping the existing example as
the illustration.

README-only change; no code touched, so nothing to test beyond the prose. I left
`CHANGELOG.md` alone since this is a documentation fix.

Fixes #920.

`RangeStep::next()` advanced with an unconditional `self.state += self.step`.
When a `--parameter-scan` range ends at (or one step below) `i32::MAX`, the
final `state + step` overflows — panicking in debug/test builds and silently
wrapping to `i32::MIN` in release (which then generates ~4 billion commands).

The fix tracks completion with a `finished` flag and computes the step check as
`end - state`, which cannot overflow because `state <= end`. Behavior is
unchanged for all existing ranges (integer and `Decimal`); only the previously
overflowing tail is now handled correctly.

### Verification

Added `does_not_overflow_near_type_max`, which collects
`RangeStep::new(i32::MAX - 1, i32::MAX, 1)`. It panics on `master`
(`attempt to add with overflow`) and passes with this change. Full suite green;
`cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy` clean.

### Summary

`--parameter-scan` panics with an integer overflow when the range ends at (or one step below) `i32::MAX`.

### Minimal reproduction

```
hyperfine --parameter-scan x 2147483646 2147483647 'true'
```

- **Debug/test builds:** panics with `attempt to add with overflow`.
- **Release builds:** the addition wraps from `i32::MAX` to `i32::MIN` instead of panicking, so the iterator keeps going and hyperfine tries to generate ~4 billion commands (effectively a hang / OOM).

### Cause

`--parameter-scan` parses `min`/`max` as `i32` (`src/command.rs`), and the `MAX_PARAMETERS` (100,000) cap is only enforced at construction via `size_hint`. A short range positioned near `i32::MAX` passes that cap, but the iterator's `next()` in `src/parameter/range_step.rs` does an unconditional `self.state += self.step`. On the final element `state == i32::MAX`, so `state + step` overflows — panicking in debug and wrapping in release.

### Expected

The scan should yield the in-range values and stop, without overflowing, regardless of where the range sits in the `i32` domain.

I have a small fix + regression test ready and will open a PR referencing this issue.
body.title: panic: integer overflow in `--parameter-scan` near i32::MAX

Closes #607.

This adds an `--import-json <file>` flag that loads benchmarks from a JSON file previously written by `--export-json` and folds them into the current run. The imported entries are not re-executed: they appear in the relative speed comparison and in every export format alongside any commands given on the command line.

```sh
hyperfine 'old-binary args' --export-json baseline.json
hyperfine --import-json baseline.json 'new-binary args'
```

`--import-json` can be specified more than once to combine several files. It can also be used on its own (without any commands) to convert a saved JSON run into another export format, which is the use case @dkaszews mentioned on the issue.

## Implementation notes

- `BenchmarkResult` now derives `Deserialize` in addition to `Serialize`. The fields that `--export-json` skips serialize as `default` so the existing on-disk schema parses without loss.
- A new `src/import/` module reads the JSON and reconstructs `BenchmarkResult` values. `command_with_unused_parameters` is not part of the on-disk schema, so it falls back to `command` when missing.
- The scheduler grew a small `add_imported_results` entry point. Imported results are pushed onto its results vector before any live benchmark runs, so they participate in `print_relative_speed_comparison` and in all configured exporters.
- Live benchmarks now carry a separate `display_number` so the `Benchmark N:` headers continue counting from the imported tail rather than restarting at 1. The original `number` field still indexes the per-command option arrays (`command_output_policies`, prepare, conclude), keeping that bookkeeping unchanged.
- `--command` is no longer required when `--import-json` is supplied, so a saved file can be replayed (or re-exported) without inventing a dummy command.

## Tests

- Unit tests under `src/import/mod.rs`: a JSON round-trip (re-emit a `BenchmarkResult` via serde and reload it), tolerance for missing optional fields, and a friendlier error for a missing path.
- Integration tests in `tests/integration_tests.rs` covering: import + a live command, import-only, multiple `--import-json` flags in the same invocation, and the missing-file error message.

Output looks like:

```
Benchmark 1: sleep 1.0 (imported)
Benchmark 2: sleep 2.0 (imported)
Benchmark 3: sleep 1.5
  Time (mean ± σ):      1.500 s ±  0.000 s    [User: 0.000 s, System: 0.000 s]
  Range (min … max):    1.500 s …  1.500 s    10 runs

Summary
  sleep 1.0 ran
    1.50 ± 0.00 times faster than sleep 1.5
    2.00 ± 0.00 times faster than sleep 2.0
```

## Summary

When using `--ignore-failure` with parameter scans, some parameter combinations may fail (non-zero exit code) and produce misleadingly fast times that skew the relative speed comparison. A command that errors out in 10ms shouldn't appear as "fastest" when comparing against commands that ran successfully for 2s.

This adds a `--filter-failed` flag that excludes benchmark results with any non-zero exit code from the relative speed comparison in the terminal summary output.

### Usage

```sh
hyperfine --ignore-failure --filter-failed \
  --parameter-list size 100,1000,10000 \
  'my-tool --size {size}'
```

### What it does

- Adds `BenchmarkResult::has_failure()` method that checks for non-zero or missing exit codes
- When `--filter-failed` is set, filters results before computing relative speeds in the summary
- JSON/CSV exports are unaffected (they still contain all results with exit codes for post-processing)
- If filtering leaves fewer than 2 results, the comparison is simply not shown

### What it doesn't do

- Does not modify `--ignore-failure` behavior — the two flags are independent
- Does not affect intermediate benchmark output or export formats

### Tests

- 5 new tests: 4 for `has_failure()` edge cases, 1 for the filtering behavior in relative speed comparison

Closes #591
body.title: Add --filter-failed to exclude failed results from speed comparison

Currently, `hyperfine` seems to either abort when a command fails even once, or it treats failures the same as successes.

I'd like an option for either:

- ignoring the failed runs (report their number, but otherwise compute statistics as though they never happened). Some possible names for such an option: `--omit-failed-runs`, `--forget-failed-runs`, or `--skip-failed-runs`. This is slightly confusing in the presence of existing `--ignore-failed-runs`, which I think should be renamed, see #828.
- putting the failures in a different "bucket", reporting the statistics for the successful runs and failed runs separately.


### Out of scope (as far as I'm concerned), but maybe worth discussing.

There is also a potential feature of bucketing results based on other data, say the exact exit code, or whether it takes more than X seconds, but that's less important to me now.

Another possibility that I'd consider out of scope is automatically finding the buckets, e.g. trying to fit a sum of Gaussian distributions instead of one Gaussian distribution onto the measurements.

I am trying to benchmark a test run that includes a test that is flaky and sometimes deadlocks (around 10% of the time). Successful runs take about 3 minutes, unsuccessful ones take forever. So, I do:

```
hyperfine --warmup 1 --min-runs 10 -- "timeout 5m cargo nextest run"
```

However, when the test does deadlock in any of the 10 runs, the whole benchmark is wasted.

Currently, the `--export` variants lack short flags, forcing commands to be verbose. This issue is intended to spark discussion rather than to provide a fixed change.

Inspired by the approach used in `pandoc`, we could introduce a short flag, `-e` or `-f`, as in `-f <FORMAT>` to reduce repetition. The specific letter isn't crucial, consistency is. Here's an example:

| Current | Addition |
| - | - |
| `--export-asciidoc`</br>`--export-csv`</br>`--export-json`</br>`--export-markdown`</br>`--export-orgmode` | `-f asciidoc`</br>`-f csv`</br>`-f json`</br>`-f markdown`</br>`-f orgmode` |

###### This would align with existing flags, such as `--sort auto` and `--output null`.

There are multiple ways to implement this addition. For example, we could pass a second argument `-f asciidoc <FILE>`, or use it in combination with a new option `-f asciidoc -o <FILE>`. 

This also opens the possibility for `hyperfine` to default to a specific format based on the file extension. Namely, `-o file.md` would be equivalent to `--export-asciidoc <FILE>`, simplifying the command further. That default could be overriden by specifying the format explicitly: `-f asciidoc -o file.md`. 

That strategy could also be used with `--parameter` flags, and it may break compatibility:

| Current | Addition |
| - | - |
| `--parameter-scan`</br>`--parameter-step-size`</br>`--parameter-list` | `-P scan`</br>`-P step-size`</br>`-P list` |

Ultimately the maintainers know what's best for the project, make any adjustments you see fit 🚀
body.title: A shorter `--export` option

Suppose that I am trying to optimize a tool and I want to have a precise view of the performance impact of a given change. I can use hyperfine to compare a run of the tool with a run of a modified version of the tool, and it detects the number of iterations to perform automatically according to the duration of the first run. However, I may or may not be happy with this number of iterations, depending on how the comparison turns out to be.    The command version with two `-P` options does not work.

```
error: The following required arguments were not provided:

USAGE:

For more information try --help
```

We already have

- an **outlier detection** which is useful if a background process has interferred with a single (or a few) benchmark runs
- a "first run was significantly longer than the rest" detection which can detect **caching effects**

But there are other things that can go wrong during benchmarking. For example:

1. a sudden jump in runtime which would result in a bimodal (or multi-modal) runtime distribution. This could be caused by a long-running background process that spun up
2. a continuous trend in the runtimes. Like a slowly growing/decreasing runtime which might be caused by things like thermal throttling.

It would be nice to add more heuristics to `hyperfine` to detect these scenarios as well. The second case could maybe be handled by fitting a linear model to the runtimes and to check whether its slope is close (enough) to zero.

Hi! Cool utility, @nathanchance is using it to benchmark some of our toolchains.

I was wondering if hyperfine does anything related to disabling clock frequency scaling?

On Android, if we don't pin the cores' clocks to fixed frequency, the noise in the benchmark frequently makes the results unreliable.

```sh
set -e;

get_cpus () {
  echo -n "$(adb shell 'ls /sys/devices/system/cpu' | grep 'cpu[0-9]')"
}

set_userspace_freq() {
  #echo "setting us $1"
  shell_command="echo userspace > /sys/devices/system/cpu/$1/cpufreq/scaling_governor"
  echo -n $(adb shell $shell_command)
}

get_max_freq() {
  #echo "looking for $1"
  shell_command="cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/$1/cpufreq/cpuinfo_max_freq"
  echo -n "$(adb shell $shell_command)"
}

set_freq() {
  shell_command="echo $2 > /sys/devices/system/cpu/$1/cpufreq/scaling_setspeed"
  echo -n "$(adb shell $shell_command)"
}

verify() {
   shell_command="cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/$1/cpufreq/cpuinfo_cur_freq"
   actual_freq=$(adb shell $shell_command)
   if [ "$actual_freq" == "$2" ]; then
     echo "good"
   else
     echo "bad"
   fi
}

echo "finding number of cpus"
for cpu in $(get_cpus)
do
    #echo "$cpu"
    echo "setting cpu frequency scaling governor to userspace control"
    set_userspace_freq $cpu
    echo "finding max freqency of $cpu"
    freq="$(get_max_freq $cpu)"
    echo "setting $cpu to $freq"
    set_freq $cpu $freq
    verify $cpu $freq
done
```

Is what I usually do; I'm not sure if the same sysfs nodes are exposed on x86.

Another thing I do when benchmarking is clear the page cache rather than do warmup runs:

```sh
echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
```

I couldn't quickly tell if these are done by hyperfine, but maybe they might help?
